examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Truth Set of Predicate's Negation
examples.problem:
The shaded region below represents the truth set of a predicate $P(x),$ defined over the universal set $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Determine the region that represents the truth set of $\neg P(x).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14099575/assets/cc80d49abe6293acb1325035799dac833a9bcb8f485ed1f785f78c4e1f39b8be.png)
examples.worked_solution:
The truth set of $\neg P(x)$ is the *complement* of the truth set of $P(x){:}$

$$
T_{\neg P} = \overline{T}_P
$$

Therefore, to get the truth set of $\neg P(x),$ we take all the points that belong to $U$ and do not lie in $T_p,$ as shown below.

feedback.problem:
$\,$ $2∣x$

The predicate $P(x)$ is given above. Which of following represents $¬P(x)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
In plain English, our predicate $P(x)$ means the following:

$\,$ $2$ divides $x.$

The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

$\,$ It is not true that $2$ divides $x$, 

In other words, $2$ does not divide $x.$ Therefore, $¬P(x)$ means the following:

$\,$ $2∤x$
